bib.title: Large Language Models for Mathematical Reasoning: Progresses and Challenges

legacy_report:
SOURCE: Large Language Models for Mathematical Reasoning: Progresses and Challenges. Janice Ahn, Rishu Verma, Renze Lou, Di Liu, Rui Zhang, Wenpeng Yin (Penn State, Temple). arXiv:2402.00157v4, 16 Sep 2024 (cs.CL). The extraction shows no venue, so treat it as preprint.

COVERAGE: All 14 pages, 58,794 of 58,794 chars. The body is about chars 0-33,000 (7 pages, ending at the Conclusion). The rest is references, which I skimmed. There is no appendix. The figures captions tool returned nothing. The PDF has no result figures, only dataset tables and two small examples.

KEY FINDING FOR THE TARGET NOTE: This is a pure survey with NO measured results of its own. The extracted text has no accuracy figures, no percentages, and no benchmark numbers for CoT, PAL or PoT. I found no number about prompting that I can quote. It should not be cited for any CoT or PAL effect size. It can be cited only for the qualitative statements below and for dataset sizes. Any number the note needs for CoT or PAL has to come from the primary papers: Wei 2022, Chen 2023a (PoT), Gao (PAL). Gao's PAL paper is not cited in this survey.

CLAIMS (qualitative statements about prompting, ranked by relevance to CoT / PAL / tools / verification; none has a measured number)
- claim: CoT is described as the first method to steer LLMs to step-by-step math reasoning. Self-consistency samples multiple CoT paths and uses consistency to pick a more probable answer.
  number: none
  setup: Survey description of Wei et al. 2022 and Wang et al. 2023. No experiment.
  quote: "Chain-of-thought (Wei et al., 2022), the first time to steer the LLMs to do step-by-step math reasoning, Self- Consistency (Wang et al., 2023) tried multiple Chain-of-Thought reasoning paths and leverage the consistency mechanism to discover a more probable answer."
  where: p.3, Sec 4.2 "More advanced prompts" (about char 14,300)
- claim: Program-of-Thought splits reasoning from computation. The LM writes a program (mainly Codex) and an external computer executes it. This is the same idea as PAL, but the survey does not mention PAL by name.
  number: none
  setup: Description of Chen et al. 2023a.
  quote: "Program-of-Thought (Chen et al., 2023a) separates the computational aspect from the reasoning by utilizing a Language Model (primarily Codex) to articulate the reasoning procedure as a program. The actual computation is delegated to an external computer, responsible for executing the generated programs to arrive at the desired answer."
  where: p.3, Sec 4.2 "Using external tool"
- claim: Other tool-use patterns are listed. A Python REPL corrects CoT errors (Yamauchi 2023, ChatGPT). Codex formalizes word problems into equations for an external symbolic solver (He-Yueya 2023).
  number: none
  setup: Description only.
  quote: "Yamauchi et al. (2023) employed an external tool, specifically the Python REPL, to correct errors in Chain-of-Thought."
  where: p.3, Sec 4.2
- claim: Verification by prompting. Zhou et al. 2023a use a zero-shot prompt that makes GPT-4 Code Interpreter check its own answers with code ("explicit code-based self-verification"). MathPrompter (Imani 2023) generates algebraic expressions and checks consensus across runs to give confidence.
  number: none
  setup: Description of GPT-4 Code Interpreter and MathPrompter. No effect size reported in the survey.
  quote: "This method employs a zero-shot prompt on GPT-4 Code Interpreter to encourage it to use code to self-verify its answers."
  where: p.3, Sec 4.2
- claim: Verification by training. Cobbe et al. 2021 fine-tuned a 175B GPT-3 as a verifier that scores candidate solutions. Liu et al. 2023c observed that LLMs get more correct with multiple attempts, which hints that they can generate correct solutions but struggle to tell correct from incorrect.
  number: "175B" (verifier size only)
  setup: Fine-tuning section, described secondhand.
  quote: "fine-tuned a GPT-3 model of 175B as a verifier, assigning probabilities to solution candidates." and "observed improved correctness in LLMs with multiple attempts, which hints that LLMs might generate correct solutions while struggling to differentiate between accurate and inaccurate ones."
  where: p.4, Sec 4.3 "Learning an answer verifier"
- claim: Few-shot prompting is unstable. Few-shot GPT-3 can fall to near chance depending on the in-context examples, and more so on hard sets such as TABMWP. PromptPG learns to select examples via policy gradient.
  number: none ("near chance")
  setup: GPT-3, TABMWP, secondhand from Lu et al. 2023b.
  quote: "few-shot GPT-3's performance is susceptible to instability and may decline to near chance levels due to the reliance on in-context examples."
  where: p.4, Sec 4.3
- claim: Showing work matters. ChatGPT's performance on math word problems changes dramatically depending on whether it must show its work. This is the closest the survey comes to a CoT-vs-no-CoT result, and it gives no figures.
  number: none
  setup: Shakarian et al. 2023, ChatGPT, MWP.
  quote: "ChatGPT's performance changes dramatically based on the requirement to show its work."
  where: p.3, Sec 4.1
- claim: Prompt and input effects. Replacing numerical expressions with English words raised ChatGPT's performance on SVAMP (An et al. 2023a). Without prompts, arithmetic performance drops. Instruction-tuned and system-message-responsive models depend on prompt type. Adversarial examples placed in few-shot prompts improve robustness (Zhou 2023b).
  number: none
  setup: Secondhand. ChatGPT / SVAMP, and Yuan et al. 2023 for arithmetic.
  quote: "substituting numerical expressions with English expressions can elevate the performance." and "Without prompts, performance drops (Yuan et al., 2023)."
  where: p.3 Sec 4.2; p.5 Sec 5.2
- claim: Arithmetic factors. Tokenization matters (T5 is worse than Galactica and LLaMA). Code and LaTeX in pretraining correlate with arithmetic skill. Scaling plateaus.
  number: "30B and 120B" (Galactica gave similar outcomes at both sizes)
  setup: Yuan et al. 2023, MATH-140 arithmetic.
  quote: "a performance plateau is observed, as shown by Galactica's similar outcomes at 30B and 120B parameters."
  where: p.5, Sec 5.2
- claim: Robustness. GPT-4 stays robust to distracting information added to CMATH, while other models fail. Larger non-instruction-tuned LLMs are more sensitive to changes in the answer but not necessarily more robust. Complex problems are more vulnerable to attack.
  number: none
  setup: Wei et al. 2023 (CMATH), Stolfo et al. 2023, Zhou et al. 2023b (RobustMath).
  quote: "Their findings reveal that GPT-4 can maintain robustness while other models fail."
  where: p.5, Sec 5.1
- claim: Dataset sizes (the only numbers in the text). GSM8K 8.5K, MATH 12.5K with difficulty levels 1-5, PRM800K 12K with step labels, MATH-140 has 401 expressions in 17 groups. TabMWP is 38K.
  number: 8.5K, 12.5K, 12K, 401 / 17, 38K
  setup: Dataset overview tables. These are not results.
  quote: "GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) 8.5K M Linguistically diverse" and "MATH-140 (Yuan et al., 2023) contains 401 arithmetic expressions for 17 groups."
  where: p.2, Table 1 and Sec 3.1

LIMITS
- The survey reports no experiments, no comparison table of methods, and no accuracy for any technique.
- Its taxonomy has three levels: prompting frozen LLMs, strategies enhancing frozen LLMs, and fine-tuning.
- The authors concede three challenges. Generalization is poor across datasets, grade levels and problem types. LLMs are brittle: answers change with phrasing, the same question gives different answers across trials (different reasoning paths), and models are vulnerable to adversarial inputs. CoT ignores the needs of human learners, e.g. students.
  quote: "for identical questions, an LLM may yield different final answers through distinct reasoning paths during multiple trials."
- The method coverage is dated. It covers GPT-3, ChatGPT, GPT-4, GPT4V, Bard and Claude-2 era work (2023). It predates reasoning models and RL-trained long CoT.
- It describes work secondhand, so it adds nothing beyond the primary papers.

BUILDS ON: Wei et al. 2022 (CoT); Wang et al. 2023 (self-consistency); Chen et al. 2023a (Program of Thoughts); Cobbe et al. 2021 (GSM8K and verifiers); Lewkowycz et al. 2022 (Minerva); Zhou et al. 2023a (code-based self-verification); Imani et al. 2023 (MathPrompter); Yamauchi et al. 2023; He-Yueya et al. 2023; Wu et al. 2023 (MathChat). Related surveys: Frieder 2023a, Chang 2023, Testolin 2023, Lu 2023c, Liu 2023b.

CODE: none. The only code-like items are the worked CoT example (Beth's cookies, GSM8K-style rationale with <<4*2=8>> calculator annotations, p.2) and the Q/E/A example (Jack's pens).

FIGURES: none usable. The caption tool returned nothing. The PDF has only Tables 1-3 (dataset lists) and a geometry triangle diagram.

PROBLEMS: No extraction faults in the body. No embedded instructions found. The only mid-text noise is the layout of the tables. For the note, I suggest citing this survey only as a "sharpens"-type source for the CoT and PoT descriptions, the tool-plus-verification taxonomy, and the brittleness and sampling-variance caveat. It supports no quantitative claim. Text dump saved at /tmp/ahn.txt.
